title: Measuring and Improving Transfer of Neural Surrogates for Vehicle Aerodynamics
authors: Favour Nerrise, Julian Busch, Gurpreet Singh Hora, Martin Sipka, Danielle C. Maddix, Georgia Olympia Brikis
abstract: Neural surrogates for external vehicle aerodynamics are fast alternatives to physics-based computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations. Their foundational limitation is a lack of zero-shot generalization across vehicle classes, which results in an expensive, custom training campaign for each new vehicle design. Similar to pretrained models in other fields, a pretrained surrogate should adapt to a new vehicle class using only a few simulations and stay accurate on its pretraining domain. No prior study has systematically tested this transfer behavior. We conduct a large-scale, controlled benchmarking study on five DrivAerML-pretrained surrogates across four independent target datasets. These datasets differ from the source in geometry, CFD solver, turbulence model, and flow conditions. We find that fine-tuning these surrogates outperforms training from scratch in fewer than half of the comparisons and lowers the accuracy of the surrogate on its source dataset. We introduce GeoReplay, a geometry- and gradient-aligned source replay that keeps source simulations resembling the target in training and applies their updates only when they agree with the target gradient. A risk bound separates geometric coverage from differences in the simulated physics, and we prove that every sufficiently small GeoReplay step decreases the target training objective. GeoReplay lowers the source error of fine-tuning in 77 of 80 settings and matches its target accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: GeoReplay preserves pretrained vehicle-aerodynamics knowledge while matching standard fine-tuning accuracy on new target datasets.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method could help engineers adapt CFD surrogates to new vehicle classes without sacrificing accuracy on previously learned designs.
method: Benchmark five DrivAerML-pretrained surrogates on four independent target datasets.
Replay source simulations with geometries resembling the target, applying source updates only when aligned with the target gradient.
Separate geometric coverage from simulated-physics differences in a risk bound and prove target-objective descent for sufficiently small GeoReplay steps.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 80 settings, GeoReplay lowers source error relative to fine-tuning in 77 while matching target accuracy; standard fine-tuning beats training from scratch in fewer than half of comparisons.
infographic.watch_item: The descent guarantee concerns the target training objective, not unseen-vehicle accuracy, so deployment still requires validation under geometry and physics shifts.
infographic.paper_title: Measuring and Improving Transfer of Neural Surrogates for Vehicle Aerodynamics

title: Nonlinearly Causal General-Relativistic Superfluid Hydrodynamics: Simulating Vortex Dynamics in Neutron-Star Interiors
authors: Yuan Feng, Elias R. Most, Lorenzo Gavassino
abstract: Neutron stars provide a natural laboratory for superfluid matter under extreme conditions. Its nonlinear dynamics is central to pulsar glitches, their possible links to fast radio bursts, and tidal interactions in inspiralling binaries. We develop a general-relativistic superfluid hydrodynamics framework incorporating entrainment, vortex forces, and line energy, and derive, for the first time, necessary and sufficient conditions for nonlinear causality and strong hyperbolicity. We also show that commonly used dissipative, force-balanced formulations without line tension are generically ill-posed at short wavelengths because of the Donnelly-Glaberson instability. Exploiting the analogy between vortex arrays with tension and force-free electrodynamics, we recast vortex dynamics in terms of effective electric and magnetic fields and drift velocities. This motivates a new finite-volume scheme combining constrained transport of superfluid vorticity with implicit electric-field evolution, enabling stable numerical evolution of the full system. We validate the scheme using an exact solution to the relativistic superfluid Riemann problem and Kelvin-wave dispersion relations, among other tests. Finally, we simulate dynamical, global general-relativistic two-fluid neutron-star equilibria, validate their oscillation modes, and present the first simplified calculation of superfluid interior spin-down with prescribed vortex release and repinning. The resulting stationary state retains both a net twist in the vortex array and residual differential rotation of the superfluid. Our framework thus enables nonlinear numerical studies of general-relativistic superfluid dynamics in neutron-star interiors.

infographic.key_insight: A general-relativistic superfluid framework establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for nonlinear causality and strong hyperbolicity, enabling stable simulations of neutron-star vortex dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework provides a computational foundation for studying superfluid transport, pulsar glitches, and tidal dynamics in neutron stars.
method: Model entrainment, vortex forces, and vortex line energy in relativistic two-fluid hydrodynamics.
Recast vortex dynamics using effective electric and magnetic fields inspired by force-free electrodynamics.
Combine finite-volume evolution with constrained transport of vorticity and implicit electric-field updates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validation includes an exact relativistic superfluid Riemann solution, Kelvin-wave dispersion relations, and neutron-star oscillation modes; a simplified spin-down simulation retains vortex twist and residual differential rotation.
infographic.watch_item: The spin-down calculation prescribes vortex release and repinning, so it does not yet establish predictive glitch dynamics.
infographic.paper_title: Nonlinearly Causal General-Relativistic Superfluid Hydrodynamics: Simulating Vortex Dynamics in Neutron-Star Interiors

title: Singular layer neural networks for the Navier-Stokes equations at small viscosity
authors: Teng-Yuan Chang, Gung-Min Gie, Youngjoon Hong, Chang-Yeol Jung
abstract: We develop neural network methods for the two-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations at a small viscosity $\varepsilon > 0$, whose accuracy is uniform in $\varepsilon$ and whose residual is evaluated on a grid that does not resolve the vorticity boundary layer. In the vorticity-stream function formulation with the slip boundary conditions, a vorticity layer of width $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ forms along the walls. The trial function of the singular layer Physics-Informed Neural Network (sl-PINN) contains the corrector of the asymptotic analysis, together with the law that fixes its amplitude at the wall. The amplitude is tied to the wall trace of the network itself, so that the method requires no a priori knowledge of the limit solution. The sl-PINN keeps the error uniform in $\varepsilon$ over six decades, for the Stokes and the Navier-Stokes equations alike, although in the latter the wall trace travels with the flow and is not known in advance. An enrichment that uses the thin scale but leaves the profile and the amplitude of the layer free deteriorates as $\varepsilon\to0$. Since the corrector carries the layer analytically, the Laplacian in the residual can be discretized by a finite volume flux difference on a coarse grid. The resulting singular layer Finite Volume Neural Network (sl-FVNN) attains the same uniform accuracy as the sl-PINN, to within the scatter of the random seed, at about half the cost of a training step. The combination of the asymptotic corrector with the coarse-grid finite volume discretization is the main result of this article.

infographic.key_insight: Embedding an asymptotic boundary-layer corrector in neural trial functions preserves accuracy at small viscosity without a grid that resolves the thin vorticity layer.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce the cost of viscosity-robust flow simulation by representing near-wall layers analytically rather than refining the residual grid.
method: Use a singular-layer PINN for 2D incompressible flow in vorticity–stream function form with slip boundary conditions.
Tie the analytical corrector’s amplitude to the network’s wall trace, avoiding prior knowledge of the limit solution.
Replace the residual Laplacian with coarse-grid finite-volume flux differences to obtain sl-FVNN.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports viscosity-uniform errors over six decades for Stokes and Navier–Stokes tests, with sl-FVNN matching sl-PINN accuracy within seed scatter at about half the training-step cost.
infographic.watch_item: The demonstrated setting uses 2D slip-wall flows; extending it to other boundary conditions or geometries may require new asymptotic correctors.
infographic.paper_title: Singular layer neural networks for the Navier-Stokes equations at small viscosity

title: Onset of three dimensionality in transonic shock boundary layer interaction over a natural laminar flow airfoil
authors: Abhijeet Guha, Aditi Sengupta
abstract: The development of three-dimensionality in transonic shock--boundary-layer interactions (SBLI) can significantly influence the aerodynamic response of natural laminar flow (NLF) airfoils, yet the associated vorticity dynamics remain insufficiently understood. The present study investigates the short-time evolution of transonic SBLI over the SHM1 NLF airfoil using high-fidelity three-dimensional (3D) simulations at three operating conditions reported by Fujino et al., Natural-laminar-flow airfoil development for a lightweight business jet, J. Aircraft 40, 609-615 (2003). The selected cases represent three distinct operating regimes: the initial development of a normal shock, drag divergence, and shock-induced separation. Comparisons with previously reported two-dimensional (2D) simulations establish the temporal interval over which the spanwise-averaged 3D flow remains close to the corresponding 2D evolution, while departures in surface pressure and skin-friction responses identify the subsequent development of 3D effects within the SBLI region. The temporal evolution of volume-integrated streamwise and wall-normal enstrophies further characterizes the development of the associated 3D vortical field. The compressible enstrophy transport equation (CETE) is subsequently employed to examine the mechanisms governing the evolution of the 3D vortical field. Viscous and compressibility-related terms dominate the normalized enstrophy budget during the early evolution, while vortex stretching remains a minor contribution in the normal-shock and drag-divergence regimes but becomes appreciable, albeit intermittently, with the development of shock-induced separation. Across the three operating regimes, the same principal enstrophy-transport mechanisms remain active, but their relative contributions to the normalized budget are redistributed with the SBLI topology.

infographic.key_insight: Early three-dimensional vorticity evolution in transonic shock–boundary-layer interaction is dominated by viscous and compressibility effects, with vortex stretching becoming intermittently appreciable during shock-induced separation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding the onset of three-dimensional effects can inform aerodynamic assessment of natural laminar flow airfoils near drag divergence and shock-induced separation.
method: Run high-fidelity 3D simulations of the SHM1 airfoil in normal-shock, drag-divergence, and shock-induced-separation regimes.
Compare spanwise-averaged 3D pressure and skin friction with previously reported 2D simulations.
Track streamwise and wall-normal enstrophy and analyze the compressible enstrophy transport budget.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three operating conditions, the simulations identify an initial interval of near-2D evolution followed by departures in surface responses and regime-dependent redistribution of enstrophy-budget contributions.
infographic.watch_item: The study covers short-time evolution on one airfoil at three operating conditions, so long-time behavior and broader generalization remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Onset of three dimensionality in transonic shock boundary layer interaction over a natural laminar flow airfoil

title: HAVAPlot: A Web-Based Scientific Visualization and Post-Processing Platform
authors: Ozgur Tumuklu
abstract: This paper presents HAVAPlot, a browser-based framework for scientific visualization and post-processing of numerical simulation data. Operating entirely within the user's browser, HAVAPlot requires no software installation or data uploads while supporting mesh-based and tabular datasets beyond computational fluid dynamics. The framework directly reads native OpenFOAM cases, including polyhedral meshes, ASCII and binary fields, boundary data, and Lagrangian particles, as well as legacy and XML VTK files and tabular datasets. It provides line, contour, and three-dimensional plots; exact polyhedral slicing; boundary extraction; variable calculations; customizable color scales; symmetry mirroring; zoomed insets; streamlines; isosurfaces; particle visualization; and vector PDF/EPS and data export. The underlying numerical algorithms are independently verified. Cell centers and volumes agree with an independent implementation of OpenFOAM's geometric algorithm, while 6.1 million field values across four two-dimensional, axisymmetric, and three-dimensional production cases are reproduced to machine precision. For analytical fields on distorted hexahedral meshes, cell-to-point interpolation exhibits second-order convergence in the interior and first-order convergence at boundaries. Meshes containing 250,000 cells load in at most 1.3 seconds. Applications to an impinging supersonic jet, hypersonic cylinder flow, a hybrid particle-continuum cold-spray nozzle, a three-dimensional gas-bearing film, and supersonic cone flow demonstrate the framework's capabilities.

infographic.key_insight: HAVAPlot enables browser-only scientific visualization and post-processing of simulation data without software installation or data uploads.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can inspect native OpenFOAM, VTK, and tabular datasets locally and export publication-ready vector graphics and processed data.
method: Read native OpenFOAM meshes, fields, boundaries, and particles alongside VTK and tabular data.
Apply exact polyhedral slicing, variable calculations, streamlines, isosurfaces, and particle visualization.
Verify mesh geometry, field reading, and interpolation against independent implementations and analytical fields.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four production cases, 6.1 million field values were reproduced to machine precision; interpolation showed second-order interior and first-order boundary convergence, and 250,000-cell meshes loaded in at most 1.3 seconds.
infographic.watch_item: Browser memory and performance for datasets substantially larger than the reported 250,000-cell loading benchmark remain unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: HAVAPlot: A Web-Based Scientific Visualization and Post-Processing Platform

title: Stochastic Representation-Inspired Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Incompressible Fluid Flows
authors: Zihao Guo, Zhongmin Qian
abstract: The effectiveness of neural networks in solving partial differential equations depends not only on their approximation capability but also on the suitability of their representations for the underlying solutions. Motivated by stochastic integral representations of incompressible fluid flows and the associated Biot--Savart kernel, we propose a Biot--Savart-informed (i.e. physics-informed) neural network (BS-PINN) for the incompressible Navier--Stokes equations. By extracting a rational profile from a regularized Biot--Savart kernel, we construct a smooth activation function with fixed and learnable kernel scales. Both variants retain the conventional velocity--pressure formulation and physics-informed training framework, allowing the influence of the activation function to be examined independently. We evaluate the method on five benchmarks, including Kovasznay flow, cylinder wake, three-dimensional Beltrami flow, Taylor--Green vortex, and double shear layer. Across 21 benchmark--architecture comparisons, both variants consistently reduce the combined velocity error relative to the conventional $\tanh$-based PINN, achieving mean relative error reductions of 31.7\% and 33.2\%, respectively. Improvements are also observed in reported pressure and vorticity errors. Notably, the double-shear-layer experiments demonstrate improved resolution of localized shear structures and, for BS-PINN-F, qualitatively clearer vortex-roll-up patterns in the long-time simulation. These findings highlight the potential of incorporating analytical flow structures into neural-network representations for incompressible flow simulations.

infographic.key_insight: Biot–Savart-inspired activation functions improve PINN accuracy for incompressible flows while preserving the standard velocity–pressure formulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Physics-informed activation design offers a way to improve neural flow simulation accuracy and resolve localized shear structures without changing the governing-equation framework.
method: Extract a smooth rational activation profile from a regularized Biot–Savart kernel.
Test fixed-scale and learnable-scale activation variants.
Retain conventional Navier–Stokes physics-informed training to isolate activation effects.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five flow benchmarks and 21 benchmark–architecture comparisons, both variants consistently reduced combined velocity error versus tanh-based PINNs, with mean relative reductions of 31.7% and 33.2%, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish computational cost or generalization to high-Reynolds-number turbulent engineering flows.
infographic.paper_title: Stochastic Representation-Inspired Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Incompressible Fluid Flows

title: A curvature-corrected port-Hamiltonian reduced-order model for dissipative sloshing with contact-line hysteresis in low-gravity tanks
authors: Gianni Cassoni, Fabrizio Gennari, Jacopo Serafini, Pierangelo Masarati
abstract: A physics-based reduced-order model unifies curved-meniscus inertia, viscous losses and nonsmooth contact-line stick-slip in a passive port-Hamiltonian formulation for lateral sloshing in cylindrical tanks. Dirichlet-Neumann and Jacobi operators describe inertia and restoring forces, while a convex potential combines bulk, Stokes-layer and contact-line dissipation. Analytical propagation between stick-slip events supports faster-than-real-time simulation of coupled spacecraft translation and sloshing. The viscous closure agrees within 5% with a reference Stokes calculation, and the model reproduces the Henderson-Miles modal measurements and the Cocciaro hysteretic decay. Across 42 drop-tower and ground measurements, curvature correction reduces the root-mean-square frequency error from 24 to 4%. For flight and ground tests from the Middeck 0-Gravity Dynamics Experiment (MODE), frequency errors range from 0.9 to 7.1%, while ideal contact lines underestimate the damping ratios from the MODE fits by 38-87%. One hysteresis width, calibrated on the lowest orbital water excitation, predicts higher orbital excitations and the ground test with normalised force errors of 11-35%, against 149-208% for an ideal pinned line. It predicts 8.5% resonance softening against 7.3% measured, which the tested one-parameter damping laws miss. Uncertain wetting and remaining response discrepancies motivate damping ranges in spacecraft control analyses.

infographic.key_insight: A passive reduced-order sloshing model combines meniscus curvature, viscous losses and contact-line hysteresis to predict low-gravity tank dynamics more accurately.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Faster-than-real-time simulation of coupled spacecraft motion and sloshing can support control analyses that account for uncertain damping.
method: Port-Hamiltonian formulation with curvature-aware inertia and restoring operators.
Convex dissipation potential for bulk, Stokes-layer and contact-line losses.
Analytical propagation between contact-line stick-slip events.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 42 drop-tower and ground measurements, curvature correction reduced RMS frequency error from 24% to 4%; a calibrated hysteresis width yielded 11–35% normalised force errors in additional MODE tests versus 149–208% for an ideal pinned line.
infographic.watch_item: Uncertain wetting and residual response discrepancies warrant damping ranges rather than a single nominal value in spacecraft control analyses.
infographic.paper_title: A curvature-corrected port-Hamiltonian reduced-order model for dissipative sloshing with contact-line hysteresis in low-gravity tanks

title: Direct Numerical Simulation of Vortex-Induced Instability Over a Semi-Infinite Flat Plate with Discrete Roughness
authors: Aditi Sengupta, Tapan K. Sengupta, Vajjala K. Suman
abstract: The receptivity of flow over a semi-infinite flat plate to a combination of deterministic free stream excitation and surface roughness, is investigated by solving the incompressible Navier-Stokes equation (NSE). The free stream excitation is in the form of a convecting vortex with fixed strength and sign, while the roughness element is a Gaussian bump. Two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) direct numerical simulations (DNS) are performed to determine whether the nonmodal nonlinear nature of transition, previously established for the vortex-induced instability in [Sundaram et al., Effects of free stream excitation on the boundary layer over a semi-infinite flat plate, Phys. Fluids, 32, 094110 (2020))], holds in the presence of surface roughness. The study aims to capture the fundamental differences arising due to the addition of surface roughness using instantaneous flow features, vorticity dynamics and application of nonlinear theories of receptivity. Roughness accelerates the transition process significantly, while retaining the indicator of nonmodal response, i.e. the spatio-temporal wave front (STWF). The inherently 2D nature of the vortex-induced instability evolves to three-dimensionality much faster in the presence of roughness, necessitating a 3D framework to capture the effects of roughness accurately. The cumulative response to the surface bump and convecting vortex can be separated into four stages, viz. are (i) generation of vortical disturbances at the roughness, (ii) a spatio-temporal amplification of the disturbance field, (iii) emergence and amplification of the STWF marked by sequence of unsteady separation bubbles, and (iv) emergence of turbulent flow due to merging of the unsteady separation bubbles to turbulent spots.

infographic.key_insight: A Gaussian surface bump accelerates vortex-induced transition and three-dimensional breakdown while preserving the spatio-temporal wave front associated with nonmodal response.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Predicting transition under combined surface roughness and free-stream vortices requires accounting for rapid three-dimensional disturbance growth.
method: Solve the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations using 2D and 3D direct numerical simulations.
Model excitation with a convecting vortex of fixed strength and sign and roughness with a Gaussian bump.
Analyze instantaneous flow features, vorticity dynamics, and nonlinear receptivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulations identify four stages: roughness-generated disturbances, spatio-temporal amplification, wave-front emergence with unsteady separation bubbles, and bubble merging into turbulent spots.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no quantitative transition shifts, and findings for a single Gaussian bump and prescribed vortex should not be generalized to arbitrary roughness or inflow conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Direct Numerical Simulation of Vortex-Induced Instability Over a Semi-Infinite Flat Plate with Discrete Roughness

title: $H_2$-optimal riblet profiles for turbulence suppression in channel flows
authors: Daniel W. Hartman, Armin Zare
abstract: The drag-reducing properties of streamwise-elongated surface corrugations, commonly referred to as riblets, have been extensively studied through experiments, simulations, and reduced-order modeling. Notably, the linearized Navier-Stokes framework introduced by Ran, Zare, and Jovanovic (J. Fluid Mech., vol. 906, 2021) employs volume penalization to model riblet-induced boundary conditions and predict drag reduction. These approaches typically quantify drag reduction as a function of a single geometric parameter, such as spanwise spacing or groove cross-sectional area, evaluated over fixed riblet shapes. As a result, identifying optimal riblet geometries across a broader design space often necessitates exhaustive parametric studies. To address this problem, we propose an optimization framework for the systematic design of optimal riblet shapes. Accordingly, we reformulate the volume penalization term in the linearized dynamics as a structured state-feedback operator. Targeting maximal suppression of turbulence, we pose a composite optimization problem that minimizes the steady-state variance of velocity fluctuations and riblet-induced dynamical augmentations while maintaining a constant bulk-flux. For a fixed spanwise wavelength (riblet spacing), this framework yields optimal wall-normal profiles that achieve maximal turbulence attenuation.

infographic.key_insight: An H₂-optimal design framework identifies riblet profiles that maximize turbulence attenuation at a fixed spanwise spacing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Systematic riblet-shape optimization could guide drag-reducing channel surfaces without exhaustive searches over predefined geometries.
method: Model riblets using volume penalization in linearized Navier–Stokes dynamics.
Recast penalization as structured state feedback.
Optimize velocity-fluctuation variance and riblet-induced dynamical augmentations at constant bulk flux.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports optimal wall-normal profiles for fixed riblet spacing but provides no quantitative attenuation results or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: Optimality is model-based and spacing-specific; nonlinear-flow validation is needed to establish realized drag reduction.
infographic.paper_title: $H_2$-optimal riblet profiles for turbulence suppression in channel flows

title: Theory of magneto-electrokinetics in unidirectional electrolyte flow: Hydrodynamic potential and Hall effect
authors: Yoav Tsori
abstract: We develop a theoretical framework for magneto-electrokinetic transport in dilute electrolytes under unidirectional flow and streaming current conditions. Unlike standard magnetohydrodynamics in liquid metals, where charge carriers are electrons and conductivity is typically uniform, electrolytes exhibit spatially varying ion densities and additional forces such as osmotic pressure. In steady state, the coupled Navier--Stokes, Nernst--Planck, and Poisson equations become analytically tractable. We derive a Boltzmann-like expression for ion distributions that incorporates both the electrostatic potential and a novel hydrodynamic potential arising from the magnetic field. This potential depends explicitly on the flow profile and is not screened close to the bounding walls. Applying the theory to Poiseuille flow, we derive expressions for the induced Hall potential and demonstrate its near-linear dependence on flow velocity and magnetic field strength, while remaining largely independent of salt concentration. To validate this one-dimensional framework, we analyze the two-dimensional spatial transients near the channel entrance. We demonstrate a separation of length scales: the Hall electric field and space charge adjust to the magnetic field almost instantaneously, whereas the macroscopic salt concentration wake develops over a much longer Graetz length dictated by the Péclet number. We also examine a similar flow with counterions only and no added salt, determining the resulting potential and ion distributions. This work offers new theoretical tools for understanding ion transport in microfluidic and electrochemical systems.

infographic.key_insight: A magnetic-field-induced hydrodynamic potential modifies ion distributions in flowing electrolytes, producing a Hall potential that is nearly linear in flow velocity and magnetic field strength but largely independent of salt concentration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could inform magnetic control and interpretation of ion transport in microfluidic channels and electrochemical systems.
method: Analytically couple steady-state Navier–Stokes, Nernst–Planck, and Poisson equations for unidirectional electrolyte flow.
Derive ion distributions incorporating electrostatic and hydrodynamic potentials, then apply them to Poiseuille and counterion-only flows.
Analyze two-dimensional entrance transients to assess the one-dimensional framework.
infographic.evidence_signal: Theoretical analysis predicts rapid Hall-field and space-charge adjustment versus a much longer, Péclet-dependent salt-concentration wake; the abstract reports no experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: Applicability beyond dilute electrolytes and steady unidirectional flow requires further assessment, especially near channel entrances.
infographic.paper_title: Theory of magneto-electrokinetics in unidirectional electrolyte flow: Hydrodynamic potential and Hall effect

title: Influence of an oxide cap on the combustion of aluminum particles using boundary-layer resolved simulations
authors: Hesheng Bao, Hongchao Chu, Shibam Bose, Heinz Pitsch
abstract: A distinctive feature of burning aluminum particles is the condensation of the primary combustion product, alumina, forming an oxide cap that covers part of the aluminum particle and alters the local combustion characteristics. This study systematically investigates the effects of an oxide cap on the combustion characteristics and interfacial processes of aluminum particles, using boundary-layer resolved simulations, considering variations in cap size, cap position relative to the flow direction, and the particle Reynolds number, $\mathrm{Re_p}$. The oxide cap modifies both the interfacial transfer and the surrounding combustion characteristics. Front caps enhance local evaporation near the junction between the cap and the aluminum body, whereas heat absorption by rear caps contributes to lower reaction temperatures. Variations in integrated heat release generally follow those in the evaporation rate. Based on the simulation results, the Lagrangian modeling framework was first revised for spherical particles. The film state is approximated using a 0.55-rule applied to temperature, species mass fractions, and pressure, from which the remaining thermophysical properties are derived. A simplified composition scheme enables film-state viscosity and fuel diffusivity to be pre-calculated as functions of temperature. Optimized Whitaker and Schiller-Naumann correlations were developed for the mass evaporation rate and drag force coefficient, respectively, showing good agreement with the simulation results. The framework was further extended to doublet particles with oxide caps. Accounting for the exposed aluminum area provides good evaporation predictions for rear caps, while front caps require a correction to the surface-averaged evaporation mass flux, particularly at high $\mathrm{Re_p}$.

infographic.key_insight: Oxide-cap position shapes aluminum-particle combustion: front caps enhance local evaporation near the cap–metal junction, while rear caps absorb heat and lower reaction temperatures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Cap-aware evaporation and drag models can improve Lagrangian predictions of burning aluminum particles without resolving each particle’s boundary layer.
method: Use boundary-layer-resolved simulations to vary cap size, cap orientation, and particle Reynolds number.
Approximate film conditions with a 0.55-rule and optimize Whitaker evaporation and Schiller–Naumann drag correlations.
Extend the model to capped doublet particles using exposed aluminum area and a front-cap evaporation correction.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports good agreement between optimized correlations and simulations, with exposed-area scaling predicting rear-cap evaporation well but front caps requiring an additional correction.
infographic.watch_item: Exposed-area scaling alone is insufficient for front caps, particularly at high particle Reynolds numbers; the abstract does not specify quantitative errors or validity ranges.
infographic.paper_title: Influence of an oxide cap on the combustion of aluminum particles using boundary-layer resolved simulations

title: Partitioned iterative FD-SPH for fluid-rigid-body interaction: Stability and validation for lightweight floating bodies
authors: Kumpei Tsuji, Ciara Galvin, Hiroyuki Omura, Naoto Mitsume, Mitsuteru Asai
abstract: This study assesses partitioned iterative fictitious-domain smoothed particle hydrodynamics (FD-SPH) for free-surface fluid-rigid-body interaction. Extending a strong-coupling framework for deformable structures, it combines volume-based hydrodynamic loads with Newton-Euler rigid-body updates. Within each time step, the mismatch between pressure-projected fictitious-fluid and rigid-body velocities is fed back iteratively. A fractional-step interpretation identifies conditions under which Passively Moving Solid (PMS) projection and Newton-Euler updates yield identical rigid-body velocities. Single-pass and iterative FD-SPH are compared under matched conditions. A two-dimensional settling-disk benchmark agrees with published results. In three-dimensional buoyancy-driven cube tests, single-pass coupling becomes unstable at specific gravities of 0.1 and 0.2. At 0.1, reducing the time-step size by a factor of 500 does not suppress the instability. Iterative strong coupling remains stable across the tested range of 0.1-1.0. Equilibrium heights and orientations agree with hydrostatic expectations and published stable configurations, respectively. Two- and three-dimensional wet-bed dam-break simulations reproduce experimental trends in wave elevation and floating-body heave and pitch. Two star-shaped rigid bodies demonstrate applicability to complex geometries without explicit interface reconstruction or surface-normal evaluation. All production strong-coupling simulations satisfy the prescribed relative-residual criterion at every time step before reaching the maximum coupling-iteration count. These results support iterative FD-SPH for lightweight and complex floating bodies in transient free-surface flows.

infographic.key_insight: Iterative strong coupling stabilizes FD-SPH simulations of lightweight floating bodies where single-pass coupling fails, even with much smaller time steps.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports simulation of lightweight, complex-shaped floating structures in transient free-surface flows without explicit interface reconstruction or surface-normal evaluation.
method: Combine volume-based hydrodynamic loads with Newton–Euler rigid-body updates.
Iteratively feed back the mismatch between pressure-projected fictitious-fluid and rigid-body velocities within each time step.
Analyze when Passively Moving Solid projection and Newton–Euler updates produce identical rigid-body velocities.
infographic.evidence_signal: Iterative coupling remained stable across tested cube specific gravities of 0.1–1.0, while settling-disk and dam-break benchmarks agreed with published results and experimental trends.
infographic.watch_item: Strong coupling requires repeated updates per time step; all reported production runs met the residual tolerance, but computational overhead is not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Partitioned iterative FD-SPH for fluid-rigid-body interaction: Stability and validation for lightweight floating bodies

title: Scattering by Small Ice Crystals in Turbulence: From Orientation Statistics to Retrieval Biases
authors: Himanshu Mishra, Mohd. Meraj Khan, T. Narayana Rao, Anubhab Roy
abstract: Ice-cloud retrievals from polarimetric radar, lidar and submillimeter radiometry commonly assume random orientation, horizontal alignment or a prescribed flutter angle. We link the orientation dynamics of ice crystals to their scattering. Fluid-inertial torque turns small settling crystals broadside on, and turbulent velocity gradients turn them away, so their orientation depends on the dissipation rate. We combine a closed-form orientation distribution for overdamped spheroids, including rotational diffusion and turbulence intermittency, with orientation-averaged Rayleigh, Rayleigh--Gans, T-matrix and specular scattering. Turbulence enters the scattering only through the Legendre moments of the orientation distribution. In the Rayleigh regime the specific differential phase follows crystal alignment, so assuming perfectly horizontal crystals biases ice-water-content retrievals low. Combining the specific differential phase with differential reflectivity limits this bias to $25\%$ for a single size of the shapes studied. For size distributions that span the alignment transition the bound can fail, because the two observables weight sizes differently. Depolarization adds sensitivity to higher-order moments and to intermittency. At finite size the second orientation moment mainly controls the scattering cross sections and the asymmetry parameter, and for optically soft crystals its contribution vanishes $54.7^\circ$ from the vertical. Specular returns from partly aligned plates should persist for lidars pointed $3^\circ$ from nadir. An exploratory analysis of EarthCARE lidar data finds a weakly depolarizing, low-lidar-ratio signature most frequent near $-11^\circ$C, where plates grow. Degree-scale tilt widths inferred from glints and lidar require larger crystals, near or beyond the validity range of the model.

infographic.key_insight: Turbulence alters ice-crystal alignment and scattering, causing ice-water-content retrievals that assume perfect horizontal alignment to underestimate content in the Rayleigh regime.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accounting for orientation statistics can reduce bias in radar, lidar and submillimeter ice-cloud retrievals.
method: Model spheroid orientations using settling-induced torque, turbulent gradients, rotational diffusion and intermittency.
Average Rayleigh, Rayleigh–Gans, T-matrix and specular scattering over orientation distributions.
Express turbulence effects through Legendre moments and assess retrieval biases.
infographic.evidence_signal: For single-size populations of the studied shapes, combining specific differential phase and differential reflectivity limits retrieval bias to 25%; exploratory EarthCARE lidar analysis finds a compatible signature most frequent near −11 °C.
infographic.watch_item: The 25% bias bound can fail for size distributions spanning the alignment transition because the two observables weight crystal sizes differently.
infographic.paper_title: Scattering by Small Ice Crystals in Turbulence: From Orientation Statistics to Retrieval Biases

title: Effective-dimension estimation of a minimal turbulent channel flow via IRMAE-WD
authors: Ryuto Saeki, Keita Nakamura, Koji Fukagata
abstract: The implicit rank-minimizing autoencoder with weight decay (IRMAE-WD) (Zeng et al. 2024) aims to estimate the dimension of the low-dimensional manifold underlying high-dimensional data from a sharp drop in the latent singular values of a single trained model. We apply IRMAE-WD with a three-dimensional convolutional autoencoder to velocity fields of a minimal turbulent channel flow at ${\rm Re}_τ=110$ and examine whether the drop represents the intrinsic degrees of freedom. We also compare the number of coordinates IRMAE-WD needs for a given reconstruction accuracy or smallest reproduced scale with that of proper orthogonal decomposition (POD). We find that a clear drop appears and that the reconstruction rate decreases by at most 0.01 percentage points with truncation at the drop. The drop thus marks the effective dimension of the trained representation. However, the drop position moves to the lower-dimension side as linear layers are added. In addition, the reconstruction error decreases only gradually with the number of coordinates in all but the smallest wavelength band. These results suggest that the drop position is set by the implicit regularization of the linear layers and cannot be regarded as the intrinsic degrees of freedom. In contrast, with transfer learning, the smallest number of coordinates needed for a given accuracy hardly depends on the number of linear layers and is smaller than that of POD up to a reconstruction rate of about 97%. IRMAE-WD also reproduces a given scale with fewer coordinates than POD. Above about 97%, however, POD requires fewer coordinates, mainly because IRMAE-WD reconstructs large-scale structures less precisely. Hence, when the error decreases continuously, as in the minimal channel flow, the number of coordinates needed to represent wall turbulence should be stated with the required accuracy or scale, not as a single number.

infographic.key_insight: IRMAE-WD’s latent singular-value drop identifies the trained representation’s effective dimension, not an intrinsic turbulence dimension; coordinate counts should be tied to target accuracy or scale.
infographic.engineering_relevance: IRMAE-WD can compress minimal-channel velocity fields more efficiently than POD up to about 97% reconstruction, supporting compact representations for flow modeling.
method: Apply a 3D convolutional IRMAE-WD autoencoder to minimal-channel velocity fields at Reτ = 110.
Vary the number of linear layers and truncate latent coordinates at the singular-value drop.
Use transfer learning to compare coordinate requirements against POD by reconstruction accuracy and reproduced scale.
infographic.evidence_signal: Truncation at the drop reduced reconstruction rate by at most 0.01 percentage points; IRMAE-WD reproduced a given scale with fewer coordinates than POD, but POD needed fewer above about 97% reconstruction.
infographic.watch_item: The drop shifts toward fewer dimensions as linear layers are added, so it should not be treated as a universal physical degree-of-freedom count.
infographic.paper_title: Effective-dimension estimation of a minimal turbulent channel flow via IRMAE-WD

title: Kinetic study of Reaction-Control-Jet Interference in Rarefied Hypersonic Crossflow
authors: Alexis Theofilis, Martin Grabe
abstract: A 1975 wind-tunnel study at the German Aerospace Center (DLR) of a helium jet blowing from a flat plate into a Mach 11 to 12 air crossflow at three freestream densities is revisited using two- and three-dimensional Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) computations at Knudsen numbers 0.021 to 0.125. The planar slot used in two-dimensional model computations reproduces the shock topology, the sign and two-lobed structure of the interference pressure and its trend with rarefaction, and its plate-alone boundary layer is consistent with the three-dimensional one and with a similarity solution with slip and temperature jump. However, two-dimensional simulations overpredict the peak interference pressure about twelvefold at every condition and carry it farther upstream. A resolution sweep at the most rarefied condition converges the planar interference to within 1% of its extrapolated limit. Three-dimensional DSMC reproduces the measured interference pressure at all three densities, within 25% at the lobe peak and 3 mm in its position, although two- and three-dimensional simulations overpredict the plate-alone wall pressure by 50 to 75%. Continuum breakdown around the jet persists even at the lowest Knudsen number examined. Fully three-dimensional kinetic simulations are underway to extend the present validation to a comparison of jet strength and forces over wider Knudsen number ranges, and to an examination of lateral relief as a reason for the discrepancy.

infographic.key_insight: Three-dimensional DSMC captures measured jet–crossflow interference pressure, while two-dimensional simulations reproduce its structure but overpredict the peak roughly twelvefold.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accurate prediction of reaction-control-jet interference in rarefied hypersonic flow requires resolving three-dimensional kinetic effects.
method: Revisited 1975 DLR helium-jet experiments in Mach 11–12 air crossflow.
Compared 2D and 3D DSMC at three freestream densities spanning Knudsen numbers 0.021–0.125.
Checked planar resolution convergence and plate-alone boundary layers.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across all three densities, 3D DSMC matches measured interference-pressure peaks within 25% and peak positions within 3 mm.
infographic.watch_item: Both simulation approaches overpredict plate-alone wall pressure by 50–75%, and validation of jet forces over wider Knudsen-number ranges remains ongoing.
infographic.paper_title: Kinetic study of Reaction-Control-Jet Interference in Rarefied Hypersonic Crossflow

title: Physics-based Tabulation Approach for Rotating Detonation Engines
authors: Noah Schwalb, Vansh Sharma, Shivank Sharma, Venkat Raman
abstract: High-fidelity simulations of rotating detonation engines remain computationally expensive due to the strong coupling between compressible flow dynamics and stiff chemical kinetics. The coexistence of deflagrative and detonative combustion, along with shock interactions and rapid thermodynamic changes, further challenges conventional reduced-order chemistry models. This work presents a multi-mode tabulation framework that replaces detailed chemical kinetic integration with precomputed thermochemical states and source terms while accounting for variations in the local thermodynamic state. The key novelty lies in a unified treatment of distinct combustion regimes, wherein homogeneous reactor solutions describe deflagrative combustion and post-detonation reactions up to the Chapman-Jouguet (CJ) point, while an equilibrium isentropic expansion model captures supersonic relaxation beyond the CJ state. The framework is evaluated against detailed chemistry across progressively complex configurations, including homogeneous ignition, one-dimensional detonations, and a two-dimensional rotating detonation engine (RDE). The tabulated model accurately reproduces ignition delays and captures the initiation and sustained propagation of detonation waves across varying mixture compositions. Furthermore, the framework reconstructs the complete thermodynamic evolution along an RDE streamline, including post-injection expansion, detonation, post-detonation expansion, and oblique shock interactions, directly from conserved flow variables. These results demonstrate the capability of multi-mode tabulation to represent coupled combustion, shock, and expansion processes within a single thermodynamically responsive framework, offering a promising route toward computationally efficient simulations of detonative combustion across a broad range of applications.

infographic.key_insight: A physics-based, multi-mode thermochemical table unifies combustion, shock, and expansion responses for rotating detonation engine simulations without direct integration of detailed chemical kinetics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a route to less expensive rotating detonation engine CFD while retaining key ignition, detonation, and thermodynamic behavior.
method: Replace detailed kinetic integration with precomputed thermochemical states and source terms.
Use homogeneous reactor solutions for deflagration and post-detonation reactions up to the Chapman–Jouguet state.
Use equilibrium isentropic expansion beyond the Chapman–Jouguet state and reconstruct local thermodynamics from conserved flow variables.
infographic.evidence_signal: Comparisons with detailed chemistry span homogeneous ignition, 1D detonations, and a 2D rotating detonation engine, showing accurate ignition delays, sustained detonation propagation, and reconstruction of streamline thermodynamic evolution.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no quantitative runtime gains or error bounds, leaving the practical accuracy–cost trade-off to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-based Tabulation Approach for Rotating Detonation Engines

title: PhysDial: Adapting Pretrained Video Models for PDE Simulation under Changing Physical Conditions
authors: Yilong Dai, Yiming Sun, Shengyu Chen, Jiaqi Gong, Xiaowei Jia, Runlong Yu
abstract: Simulating how physical systems respond to changing conditions is central to control, design, and scenario studies. To our knowledge, prior PDE foundation models have not been trained or evaluated on changes within trajectories. Our counterfactual test measures how far predictions move toward a changed solver branch from the same state. Models trained on fixed conditions follow changes only partly. A PDE foundation model given a condition input after pretraining barely responds. PhysDial adapts a pretrained video diffusion transformer to eight two-dimensional PDE families. Coefficients enter with the noise level, condition fields as reference frames, and equation text as a prompt. In Kolmogorov flow, switches within trajectories account for about 5% of the training samples. At matched compute, they halve the error after a change in forcing wavenumber or amplitude. A few trajectories at new amplitudes more than halve extrapolation error. Without physics pretraining, PhysDial matches or exceeds PDE foundation models under training conditions on two turbulent flows. At step 64 on the Kolmogorov test split, PhysDial has 1.07 times the solver's small-scale energy and Walrus 7.1 times. Our experiments suggest that a learned simulator uses a condition only as far as its training data make that condition necessary for prediction. Learning from trajectories that diverge under intervention can help scientific simulators predict what would happen if a system's forcing or parameters changed.

infographic.key_insight: PhysDial shows that training on trajectories with changing physical conditions helps pretrained video models predict PDE responses to interventions, rather than merely accept condition inputs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Condition-responsive learned simulators could support control, design, and what-if studies involving changes in forcing or physical parameters.
method: Adapt a pretrained video diffusion transformer to eight two-dimensional PDE families.
Encode coefficients alongside noise level, condition fields as reference frames, and equations as text prompts.
Train with within-trajectory switches and evaluate predictions against changed solver branches from the same state.
infographic.evidence_signal: In Kolmogorov flow, within-trajectory switches comprised about 5% of training samples and halved post-change error at matched compute for forcing wavenumber or amplitude changes.
infographic.watch_item: Condition responsiveness depends on training coverage; the reported two-dimensional experiments do not establish reliability for unseen interventions or three-dimensional turbulence.
infographic.paper_title: PhysDial: Adapting Pretrained Video Models for PDE Simulation under Changing Physical Conditions

title: Flux-induced condensation in a radial geometry
authors: Yoav Tsori
abstract: Stirring and shear usually suppress phase separation, but transport through a boundary can induce it. We study a binary mixture that is stable everywhere at rest and fills a two-dimensional annulus. The inner boundary is semipermeable and exchanges material with a permeate held at a fixed chemical potential, so that a steady flux of one component crosses the annulus. Although this driven system carries a steady current and produces entropy, within Model B dynamics its steady state is an equilibrium profile in an effective external field that is logarithmic in the distance from the center. Its strength is not imposed from outside but set by the permeate and the permeability of the boundary. Above a threshold driving flux, a condensed annulus forms around the inner boundary. It is bounded by a stationary front whose radius depends exponentially on the ratio of the bulk driving force to the flux. The front is pinned by the effective field and does not coarsen, and the threshold flux decreases only as the inverse logarithm of the system size. The driving flux shifts the phase lines but leaves the critical temperature unchanged. Interfacial tension gives rise to a critical nucleus and to a fold, at which the condensed state ceases to exist, with a threshold that we obtain in closed form. Numerical solutions confirm these predictions and reveal a hysteresis loop bounded by two saddle-node bifurcations. By symmetry, the theory also describes cavitation around a sink.

infographic.key_insight: A steady boundary-driven flux can condense an otherwise stable binary mixture into a stationary inner annulus, with the flux acting as an effective logarithmic field.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Boundary permeability and permeate chemical potential offer potential controls for localized phase separation in radial membrane systems.
method: Model B dynamics in a two-dimensional annulus with a semipermeable inner boundary.
Map the driven steady state to an equilibrium profile in an effective logarithmic field.
Derive condensation thresholds, front position, and interfacial-tension effects.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical solutions confirm the analytical predictions and reveal hysteresis bounded by two saddle-node bifurcations.
infographic.watch_item: The results rely on a two-dimensional radial Model B description; applicability with hydrodynamic flow or more complex geometries remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Flux-induced condensation in a radial geometry

title: Swimming formula in a linearly viscous fluid with anisotropic and odd viscosity tensors at low Reynolds number
authors: Yuto Hosaka, Kenta Ishimoto
abstract: We theoretically investigate the low-Reynolds-number hydrodynamics of a microswimmer in a linearly viscous fluid. The fluid is characterized by a viscosity tensor containing both even and odd components, and can therefore exhibit anisotropic and chiral properties absent in an isotropic Newtonian fluid. By employing the generalized Lorentz reciprocal theorem, we establish the Onsager-Casimir reciprocity for the resistance tensors of an arbitrarily shaped rigid body. We then derive a swimming formula that linearly relates the swimming velocities to the prescribed surface velocity of a microswimmer and imposed background flows. As a showcase application of the derived swimming formula, we prove that the scallop theorem holds in this class of linearly viscous fluids. Furthermore, we investigate the equations of motion for a spherical swimmer in a fluid with odd viscosity, as a representative example of the generalized linear constitutive framework. In particular, we reveal that sufficiently strong shear flows destabilize the bimodal chirotactic alignment of a microswimmer. Our results highlight how intrinsic fluid chirality and anisotropy fundamentally alter the orientational dynamics and transport phenomena of microswimmers.

infographic.key_insight: A generalized swimming formula describes microswimmers in fluids with anisotropic and odd viscosity, where the scallop theorem still holds but orientational dynamics can change.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could guide microswimmer control and transport design in chiral or anisotropic viscous media.
method: Apply the generalized Lorentz reciprocal theorem to establish Onsager–Casimir reciprocity for rigid-body resistance tensors.
Relate swimming velocities linearly to prescribed surface motion and imposed background flows.
Analyze a spherical swimmer in an odd-viscous fluid under shear.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical derivations showing that sufficiently strong shear destabilizes bimodal chirotactic alignment, without describing experimental or numerical validation.
infographic.watch_item: Applicability is restricted to low-Reynolds-number, linearly viscous fluids; nonlinear rheology lies outside the stated framework.
infographic.paper_title: Swimming formula in a linearly viscous fluid with anisotropic and odd viscosity tensors at low Reynolds number

title: Lagrangian transport driven by travelling waves in a radially deforming circular cavity
authors: Zijian Liu, Julian Olszewski, Jie Xu
abstract: A travelling deformation of a circular cavity wall can carry particles with the wave or against it. For two counter-propagating waves of azimuthal order $m$ and amplitudes $a$ and $b$, the leading axisymmetric component of the total (Lagrangian) drift scales with the intensity difference $S_3=|a|^2-|b|^2$. We obtain the radial profile of the azimuthal drift in closed form in the viscous limit, where the Womersley number $\mathrm{Wo}$ tends to zero, and by quadrature for any finite $\mathrm{Wo}>0$. The total drift is the sum of the Eulerian mean velocity and the Stokes drift. For radial wall motion with $m\ge2$ and unequal wave intensities, the total drift follows the stronger of the two waves throughout the interior in the viscous limit, although the Stokes drift changes sign with radius for all $\mathrm{Wo}$. For $m=2$ and large $\mathrm{Wo}$, the predicted total drift just inside a radially moving wall opposes the wave to leading order in wall amplitude. For the same travelling shape, the total drift there follows the wave when the wall material also moves tangentially to preserve local arc length to first order. For the radial wall at large $\mathrm{Wo}$, the near-wall profile consists of the planar Longuet-Higgins result and a closed-form curvature correction. At large $m$ the core rotation approaches Tuck's finite-Reynolds-number waving-sheet result. At $m=2$ and $\mathrm{Wo}^2=10$, moving-domain simulations recover the leading-order drift coefficients for both wall motions.

infographic.key_insight: Travelling wall waves drive particle drift set by their intensity imbalance, but near-wall transport can reverse depending on fluid inertia and how the wall material moves.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Wave-driven cavity designs must account for wall kinematics and operating frequency to control particle transport direction reliably.
method: Decompose Lagrangian drift into Eulerian mean flow and Stokes drift.
Derive closed-form viscous-limit profiles and quadrature solutions at finite Womersley number.
Compare radial-only wall motion with motion that preserves local arc length to first order.
infographic.evidence_signal: Moving-domain simulations at azimuthal order m=2 and Wo²=10 recover the leading-order drift coefficients for both wall motions.
infographic.watch_item: Predictions are leading-order in wall amplitude; accuracy for larger deformations requires further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Lagrangian transport driven by travelling waves in a radially deforming circular cavity
